deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT. The previous folio drafts uniqueness statements of the Dirichlet-principle / dissertation type. A function u on a surface T is considered. 'Satz II' is cited: if u1 - u2 vanishes on a part A of T, it vanishes everywhere. This is an identity theorem for harmonic functions. The present page opens with a remark: 'According to a statement of the highly esteemed author, this conjecture is incorrect.' The phrase 'des hochverehrten Herrn Verfassers' is unusual in a self-authored draft. It suggests Riemann is commenting on, or reporting about, someone else's text. Alternatively, the sheet may be a copy or notes by another person. Which 'Vermuthung' is meant cannot be fixed from these two pages. The rest of the page is a definition of continuity, rewritten three times, followed by a fragmentary corollary on boundedness.

(1) First version. 'z changes continuously with x in a given interval if every infinitely small change of x produces an infinitely small change of z.' Then 'geometrically expressed': for every given eps > 0, the interval [a,b] can be divided into subintervals so small that within each the difference of two values of z is (not) > eps. The manuscript as transcribed says '> eps'; the sense requires 'not > eps'. In modern terms: for every eps > 0 there exists a partition a = x0 < x1 < ... < xn = b with osc(z, [x_{k-1}, x_k]) = sup |z(s) - z(t)| <= eps for every k. Here the partition depends on eps but may be any partition.

(2) Second version. The interval is divided in an arbitrary manner into subintervals each of length < alpha. Then for every eps one can choose alpha so small that in each of these subintervals the oscillation of z is <= eps. Modern form: for all eps > 0 there is alpha > 0 such that every partition with mesh < alpha has all subinterval oscillations <= eps.

(3) Final, cleaned version. 'By "z changes continuously with x between the limits x=a and x=b" we understand: in this interval every infinitely small change of x corresponds to an infinitely small change of z; or, geometrically, for every given eps one can always choose alpha such that within every interval < alpha the difference of two values of z is never > eps.' Modern form: for all eps > 0 there is alpha > 0 such that for all s, t in [a,b] with |s - t| < alpha we have |z(s) - z(t)| <= eps. This is exactly uniform continuity on [a,b], written with the oscillation ('Schwankung') over short intervals. Versions (2) and (3) are equivalent: an interval of length < alpha is a cell of some partition of mesh < alpha. The revision from (1) to (2)/(3) replaces an existential partition statement by the universal 'every interval shorter than alpha' statement.

(4) Fragmentary corollary, struck through and rewritten several times. The best reading: 'Die Stetigkeit einer Function zieht ihre Endlichkeit mit sich' (continuity entails finiteness/boundedness). It ends: for a continuous function, 'becoming infinite' is excluded, since it would require infinitely many / an infinite limiting oscillation ('Grenzschwankung').

The argument is implicit; my completion follows. Take eps = 1 and the corresponding alpha. Choose N > (b-a)/alpha. Divide [a,b] into N pieces of length < alpha. Chaining through the endpoints gives |z(x) - z(a)| <= N for all x. Hence |z| <= |z(a)| + N, so z is bounded. An unbounded z would force infinitely many unit oscillations, or an infinite oscillation at some limit point, inside [a,b]. The 'Grenzschwankung' (limiting oscillation at a point, lim_{h->0} osc(z,(x-h,x+h))) is the notion used in Riemann's 1854 Habilitationsschrift on trigonometric series.
errors: In the first two formulations the inequality is written (as transcribed) as 'der Unterschied zweier Werthe von z > eps ist'. The intended meaning is 'not > eps' (<= eps). The final formulation correctly reads 'nie > eps'. This is a draft slip, either an omitted 'nicht' or a transcription error.

Version (1), the existence of some partition with small oscillations, is equivalent to continuity only if the subintervals are taken closed. Then each point lies in at most two adjacent cells, giving local oscillation <= 2 eps. The converse direction (continuous implies such partitions exist) needs compactness of [a,b], i.e. uniform continuity, which is not proved. If the cells are open, a step function satisfies (1) without being continuous. The author's revision to the 'every interval < alpha' form removes this ambiguity.

Defining 'continuity on [a,b]' directly as uniform continuity bypasses the theorem that pointwise continuity on a closed interval implies uniform continuity (Dirichlet 1854 lectures, Heine 1872). On an open or half-open interval the definition is stronger than ordinary continuity: 1/x on (0,1] is continuous but fails it. Boundedness then follows trivially. The remark 'Stetigkeit zieht Endlichkeit mit sich' is correct only under this uniform definition, or on a closed interval.
The final lines are too damaged and over-corrected to verify the exact claim about 'Unendlichwerden' and 'Grenzschwankung'.

results.what: Definition of continuity of z(x) on [a,b]: for every eps there is alpha such that on every subinterval of length < alpha the oscillation of z is <= eps (equivalently: every partition of mesh < alpha has all cell oscillations <= eps).
results.usually_credited_to: Dirichlet (1854 lectures on definite integrals, proof that continuous functions on closed intervals have this property); Weierstrass lectures (1860s); Heine (1872) for the published theorem and the term 'gleichmässig stetig'; Bolzano (1817/1830) for related eps-formulations

results.what: Oscillation ('Schwankung', limiting oscillation 'Grenzschwankung') as the tool for expressing continuity
results.modern_name: Oscillation of a function on an interval / at a point

results.what: Continuity (in the above uniform sense) on [a,b] implies boundedness; a continuous function cannot become infinite without an infinite oscillation
results.modern_name: Boundedness of continuous functions on a compact interval (part of the extreme value theorem)

deep.surprise_reason: The page contains a careful, self-revised eps-alpha definition of continuity on an interval, which is in fact uniform continuity, plus the easy corollary of boundedness. This is consistent with Dirichlet's 1854 lectures, which Riemann knew, and with the oscillation language of Riemann's own Habilitationsschrift. It is a nice record of the Dirichlet-Riemann circle's precision before Heine/Weierstrass, but not a new result. The explicit revision from an existential-partition form to a uniform form is a mildly interesting foundational detail.

checkable.asserts: For z = x**2 on [0,1], |z(x)-z(y)| = |x-y||x+y| <= 2|x-y|, so alpha = eps/2 satisfies the uniform definition (final formulation).

For z = 1/x on (0,1], the points 1/n and 1/(n+1) get arbitrarily close but z differs by 1, so no alpha works for eps < 1: the uniform definition fails though z is pointwise continuous, illustrating that the definition is stronger than pointwise continuity off closed intervals.
1/x is unbounded on (0,1], consistent with the claim that uniform continuity (which it lacks) would force boundedness.
sin(1/x) has limiting oscillation ('Grenzschwankung') 2 at x=0: points arbitrarily near 0 with values 1 and -1, so it violates the definition for eps < 2 on any interval touching 0.
Example of the boundedness argument: with alpha = 1/10 on [0,1], 10 cells suffice, giving |z(x)-z(0)| <= 10*eps.

transcription_corrections: Paragraph 1 and 2: the inequality should be read (or understood) as 'nicht > eps' / '<= eps'. As written, '> eps' contradicts the final formulation 'nie > eps' and the sense.
Line 1: 'Herrn' above the line is an uncertain reading of the interlinear word between 'hochverehrten' and 'Verfassers'. The word over 'hochverehrten' could also be a different honorific.

Paragraph 1: the struck words after 'jeder unendlich kleinen Änderung' are 'von x' (struck), and the insertion above line 3 is better read as 'für jede vorgegebene Größe eps'. 'zerfällt' should probably be 'zerfällt/zerlegt', a variant spelling of 'zerfällt werden kann'.

Last block: the reading should probably be 'Die Stetigkeit einer Function ... zieht ihre Endlichkeit mit sich' (continuity entails finiteness), with 'zu' struck and 'mit' inserted. The bracketed words before 'Endlichkeit' likely include 'ihre'.

Final lines: 'unendlich viele Grenzschwankungen ... entstehende' are interlinear insertions belonging to the last sentence. A plausible reading is 'Bei einer stetigen Function ist also ein Unendlichwerden, ohne dass dabei unendlich viele (eine unendliche) Grenzschwankung[en] entstehen, ausgeschlossen', but this is uncertain.
Third paragraph: 'größere' is written above 'mit x' (i.e. 'stetig mit x' with an inserted word, possibly 'größer'), and 'innerhalb der' is struck in favour of 'zwischen den Grenzen x = a u x = b'.
